summary:
Papua stands under the national framework of Indonesia, a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual sexual activity outside marriage; because same-sex marriage is not recognised in Indonesia, the provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations. Prosecutions are reported as selective rather than systematic. Papua carries no equivalent provincial criminal provision in the sourced record, but customary laws may operate alongside the national code.

Detention in Papua is the province's dominant traveller risk, and it is documented rather than speculative. A TAPOL briefing of July 2025 records 138 acts of torture or ill-treatment in detention by police and military in Maybrat and the Central Highlands between September 2021 and the first quarter of 2025, with almost no consequences for perpetrators. Victims were predominantly males under 24, together with seven women and seven minors; arrests were largely made for alleged links to armed groups or for participation in demonstrations. Deaths during torture were documented in the operation areas, and the incidents are catalogued on the 'Papuans Behind Bars' database.

The Human Rights Monitor Papua quarterly report of 31 October 2025 records killings, arbitrary detentions, torture and arrests of protesters across West Papua as security forces expand their presence, alongside the failure of accountability mechanisms and a healthcare crisis under scrutiny. That report carries no trans or LGBTI findings; the risk it evidences is general detention risk, which compounds sharply for a trans detainee held in a facility with documented ill-treatment and no redress.

Identity documents are obtainable in Papua. Since June 2021 Indonesia's Ministry of Home Affairs has run an outreach programme issuing identification papers (KTP) to transgender Indonesians, and Papua is among the provinces where trans residents have received them, alongside Banten, West Java, Central Java, East Java, North Sumatra, South Sumatra, South Sulawesi and Lampung. Only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors are recognised, and the birth gender is printed on the document unless a court order for legal gender recognition has already been obtained.
tangentialFactors:
Papua's legal position differs from the two provinces that carry their own criminal provisions against same-sex sexual activity, Aceh and South Sumatra, where punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present, including foreign visitors. Papua has no such provision, so a trans visitor here faces the national code and customary law rather than a provincial sexual-morality statute.

The national environment outside Papua is hostile in ways a visitor can trigger. Vigilante attacks on transgender people have risen, and reporting in August 2026 ties that surge to officials' public condemnations and to a presidential decree of October 2025 listing LGBTQ+ people as a non-military national threat alongside separatism and terrorism. Police raids on LGBT gatherings continue, including the June 2025 raid on a rented villa near Bogor in West Java that arrested 75 people. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction reaches any writing or audio-visual material suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment, and a bill to prohibit online content presenting LGBT behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller elsewhere in Indonesia. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested on drug charges, was reported to have been beaten by police, and died in custody; Indonesian police denied using violence. The Papua record of deaths during torture and near-total impunity places the same category of risk in a documented local setting.

No national law protects people in Indonesia from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and legal gender recognition requires sex reassignment surgery plus a judge's approval. Neither protection nor recognition is easier in Papua than elsewhere in the country.
localsOnly:
Trans Indonesians living in Papua have obtained identification papers through the Ministry of Home Affairs outreach programme running since June 2021, in common with residents of Banten, West Java, Central Java, East Java, North Sumatra, South Sumatra, South Sulawesi and Lampung. The documents carry only 'male' or 'female' descriptors, and show the birth gender unless a court order for legal gender recognition has been secured.

Papua's residents are subject to the same national penal code in force since 2 January 2026 and to customary laws that may apply alongside it. The TAPOL and Human Rights Monitor findings concern a resident population, predominantly young men and boys in Maybrat, the Central Highlands and across West Papua, arrested principally for alleged armed-group links or for demonstrating, and held in facilities where ill-treatment is recorded and accountability mechanisms do not function. Trans residents face that same detention apparatus.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sentence of the national penal code provision is stated inconsistently across the sourced material: the claim drawn from the encyclopaedia entry gives up to one year's imprisonment for sexual activity outside marriage, while other reporting on the code as it took effect on 2 January 2026 gives up to two years. The discrepancy is unresolved here and should be checked against the enacted text before publication.

No sourced material records trans-specific violence, hate-crime findings, police raids on LGBT gatherings, or LGBTI-focused reporting for Papua; the Human Rights Monitor Q3 2025 report explicitly carries none. Whether Papua's customary laws contain provisions addressing gender identity or same-sex conduct is not sourced, as is the practical availability of sex reassignment surgery and the associated court process for legal gender recognition in the province. Access to healthcare for trans people in Papua, and the effect of the reported healthcare crisis on that access, is not sourced. The 138 recorded acts in the TAPOL briefing cover Maybrat and the Central Highlands between September 2021 and Q1 2025 and are not a province-wide count.
